title: Why birds fly into glass, how patterns on glass prevent it, and the Javits Center retrofit in New York

sources.title: Reducing Bird Collisions with Buildings and Building Glass: Best Practices

sources.title: NYC's Javits Convention Center goes bird friendly! (2015-09-07)

facts.text: Birds do not see clear or reflective glass as a solid barrier.
In the daytime, when most collisions happen, birds fly toward reflections of sky, clouds or plants in the glass.
Birds also try to fly through glass to plants or sky they can see on the other side, including potted plants indoors.
At night, during spring and fall migration, bright lights on buildings can draw birds in and confuse them.
Most birds migrate at night, and collisions peak during spring and fall migration.
Many birds that hit a window seem fine and fly off, but later die of their injuries.
Scientists estimate that window collisions kill between 365 and 988 million birds a year in the United States.
About 44 percent of these deaths happen at homes and 56 percent at low-rise buildings of four to eleven stories; high-rise buildings account for less than 1 percent.
North America has about three billion fewer birds than in 1970.
A pattern on glass works if it breaks up the clear or reflective area so that birds sense they cannot fit through the gaps.
Horizontal stripes no more than 2 inches apart and vertical stripes no more than 4 inches apart have stopped most birds from hitting glass.
Very small birds such as hummingbirds need patterns spaced even more closely, about 2 inches by 2 inches.
Patterns work best on the outside surface of the glass.
Fritted glass has small ceramic dots or lines baked into it; people can still see through it, and it also cuts heat and glare.
Some birds can see ultraviolet light, so glass with ultraviolet patterns can warn them while looking almost clear to people.
Cheap fixes include cords hung outside windows less than 4 inches apart, paint or tape patterns, and screens.
The Javits Center, a large convention center in Manhattan, was the first major building in New York City to be refitted with bird-friendly glass.
The Javits Center's renovation took five years, cost about half a billion dollars, and used glass with a dotted pattern.
After the renovation, bird collisions at the Javits Center fell by about 90 percent.
The renovated Javits Center also uses about 26 percent less energy, and its new green roof attracts nesting birds.
Since 2019, New York City has required new buildings and major renovations to use bird-friendly design and materials.
In fall 2021 more than 200 dead birds were found outside four buildings in Lower Manhattan after bright lights confused them.
